extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and students of scientific method (readers of Baconian methodology)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles (Baconian) for discovering causes, forms, and methods to transform or understand natural bodies; covers what counts as true knowledge, desirable practical precepts, and two complementary kinds of axioms for scientific operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of aims: human power vs human knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: To generate and superinduce a new nature or natures upon a given body is the labor and aim of human power; to discover the form or true difference of a given nature (the source from which it emanates) is the labor and discovery of human knowledge. Two subordinate labors follow: transforming concrete bodies from one to another, and discovering the latent/uninterrupted process from the manifest efficient and subject up to the given form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designate whether a project aims at practical transformation (engineering/operative work) or at discovering underlying forms (theoretical understanding). Treat the subordinate tasks (practical transformation; tracing latent processes) as secondary but distinct objectives. Examples: superinducing yellow of gold on silver (practical), tracing the generation of plants from juices/seeds (latent process).

rubrics_metrics.name: True knowledge must be deduced from causes; four-fold causes
rubrics_metrics.description: True knowledge is that which is deduced from causes. The division of four causes (matter, form, efficient, end/final cause) is accepted, though the final cause corrupts the sciences except in human affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor causal explanations grounded in observable relations. Be cautious about invoking final causes for natural phenomena (they often corrupt scientific inquiry), reserving teleological reasoning for human interactions. Explicitly identify which cause (matter, form, efficient, end) your explanation targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of discovering forms (laws) as foundation of theory and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of the 'form' (the law or specific principle) of a nature is the foundation of both theory and practice; a law (form) in each science underlies and enables both explanation and operative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work by whether it seeks or establishes forms/laws with generality across subjects rather than merely cataloguing particular efficient/material causes. Knowing forms permits unifying apparently distinct substances and enables genuinely novel operations that mere empirical recipes would not yield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a true form
rubrics_metrics.description: A true form is such that when it is assigned the particular nature infallibly follows; it is always present when that nature is present, and inherent in the whole of it. If the form is removed the particular nature infallibly vanishes; it is absent whenever that nature is absent. A true form deduces the particular nature from some more known source of essence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these criteria to test candidate explanations: check presence/absence correlation, counterfactual removal, and derivation from a more known substrate. The form should both explain and be diagnostic of the phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for practical precepts: certain, free, and preparatory (relation to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine and perfect rule of practice should be certain (neither fail nor deceive), free (not restrictively tied to particular means unavailable to practitioners), and preparatory or related to practice (approachable and not more difficult than the effect required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or creating practical procedures, ensure they are reliable, allow alternative means, and are feasible—prefer precepts that get closer to practicable operations rather than abstract, highly specialized instructions. Anti-patterns: precepts that are deceptive, tie users to rare materials/methods, or are more difficult than the target effect itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of axioms/rules for transformation: primary (simple natures) and secondary (latent process)
rubrics_metrics.description: First kind: axioms that regard the body as an aggregate of simple natures (produce or combine simple properties like yellowness, weight, ductility). Second kind: axioms that trace the latent, continuous process in concrete bodies from original matter to the perfected subject (series of generation, nutritive processes, animal motion, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and state whether a method relies on decomposing into simple measurable properties (primary) or on reconstructing continuous natural processes (secondary). Primary axioms underpin transformative power over many domains; secondary/latent-process inquiries are often more immediate/promising for particular transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary-method requirement: start from constant, universal aspects (simple natures)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary method sets out from what is constant, eternal, and universal in nature (simple natures) and thereby opens broad paths to human power; by acquiring forms/methods for simple natures one can aim to unite them to produce complex substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer methods that identify universal/simple constituent natures and their operations. Be aware that combining many simple natures can be difficult and constraining; list component simples (e.g., in gold: yellowness, heaviness, malleability) when designing synthetic procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Latent-process inquiry: investigate minute, continuous, often imperceptible operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Latent processes are continued operations that often escape the senses; inquiries should determine what is lost, remains, added, diluted, contracted, united, separated, continuous, broken off, what urges forward or impedes, what predominates or is subservient, and similar circumstances across generations, transformations, nutritive processes, voluntary motion, and articulate sound production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying generation, transformation, and physiological/biological processes, probe the small-scale, continuous causal steps (including those below sensory detection). Design experiments to reveal intermediate steps, rates (quick/slow), precedences, and agents of production or governance of motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-specific applicability: deductive method vs experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: In mechanics and general sciences, causes often compound their effects so that one can often deduce consequences à priori; in chemistry and physiology, causes unite to form distinct substances and introduce unforeseen laws and combinations, making deductive method inapplicable and forcing reliance on experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess method choice by domain: use deductive reasoning where compositional causes permit reliable a priori inference (e.g., classical mechanics), but rely on empirical/inductive experiment in domains where emergent combinations yield novel behaviors (chemistry, physiology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use primary axioms for non-manipulable or celestial phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In sciences where man cannot act upon the subject (e.g., astronomy), investigation of facts and knowledge of causes must be referred to primary and universal axioms concerning simple natures (for example, the nature of spontaneous rotation) before attempting to decide questions like whether earth or heaven revolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For observational-only domains, ground inference in general axioms about simple natures rather than speculative particulars; seek universal explanatory principles applicable despite lack of experimental intervention.
